## **Understanding Medical Records Requests for Personal Injury Cases in Omaha**


Medical records are the evidentiary foundation of every personal injury claim. They document the nature and extent of injuries, establish causation, support damages calculations, and give you the factual basis for demand preparation and settlement negotiation.


A single PI case may require requests to multiple providers, and complex injury cases can involve many facilities, each with its own authorization requirements, submission methods, and processing timelines. Without a system, tracking those requests gets unwieldy quickly.


What you need extends past clinical notes:


-


Treatment records including emergency room visits, surgical reports, and follow-up care


-


Billing records for damages calculation and lien resolution


-


Imaging files, meaning the actual discs rather than radiology reports alone


-


Pharmacy records to identify prescribing physicians and medication history


-


Therapy notes from physical therapy, occupational therapy, and mental health providers


## **HIPAA Compliance: Essential Authorization Forms for Medical Records**


### **What a HIPAA Authorization Does**


HIPAA gives individuals a right to access their protected health information, generally requiring action within 30 calendar days under[45 CFR 164.524](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-C/part-164/subpart-E/section-164.524) . Attorneys commonly obtain records a different way: through a client-signed authorization under 45 CFR 164.508, an individual-directed access request where applicable, or lawful judicial process. The requirements depend on which mechanism you use, so pick one and follow its rules rather than blending them.


### **Key Elements of a Compliant Release Form**


Under[45 CFR 164.508](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-C/part-164/subpart-E/section-164.508) , a valid authorization generally includes:


-


A meaningful description of the information to be used or disclosed


-


Identification of who may make the disclosure


-


Identification of who may receive it, meaning your firm and the attorney of record


-


The purpose of the disclosure


-


An expiration date or expiration event


-


The individual's signature and date, plus a representative's authority where applicable


-


Required statements on revocation, conditioning of treatment or payment, and possible redisclosure


Providers routinely ask for more. A patient's date of birth and address, your firm's fax number, the exact facility address, a specific date range, and a wet signature are common facility requirements rather than federal core elements, and electronic signatures are acceptable in many cases. Build the form to satisfy the facility, but do not mistake its preferences for the legal standard.


On sensitive categories, do not simply check every box. Authorize the categories the representation legitimately needs and that your client has agreed to release, and account for the extra rules that apply: psychotherapy notes receive special HIPAA protection, and certain substance use disorder records carry additional federal requirements.

## **Streamlining Medical Record Retrieval: Tips for Personal Injury Lawyers**


### **Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them**


A rejected authorization can require correction and resubmission, with the provider's processing period beginning from the valid or completed request. Before submitting, verify:


-


The patient signature is present and legible


-


An expiration date or event is clearly stated


-


Any sensitive categories relevant to the representation are expressly authorized, with whatever additional consent federal or state law requires


-


The provider name and address match exactly


-


The date range covers all relevant treatment periods


**Submission method matters.** Online portals generally process fastest, followed by email and fax. Nebraska Medicine specifically advises allowing 7 to 10 days for mailed record delivery, so build postal time into any mailed request.


### **A Working Follow-Up Schedule**


The sequence below is an internal best-practice workflow, not a statutory escalation framework. Nebraska's copy deadline under §71-8403 is 30 days, so early contact is a courtesy check rather than an assertion that the provider is late.


-


**First week:** call to confirm receipt and get an estimated completion date


-


**Second week:** email the records supervisor with a copy of your authorization


-


**Approaching 30 days:** follow up in writing, citing the applicable Nebraska provision


-


**After the statutory period:** escalate to the facility's compliance officer or patient advocate and consider a formal demand


That manual cycle eats staff time. Codes Health automates persistent provider outreach across calls, faxes, emails, and portals until materials arrive, freeing your team for case strategy.


## **Ensuring Completeness: What to Look for in Retrieved Medical Records**


Receiving records is not the same as receiving complete records. Before closing a retrieval, verify:


-


All requested date ranges are covered


-


Treatment notes and billing records are both included


-


Imaging discs are enclosed, not just radiology reports


-


All pages are legible with no cutoffs


-


Authorized sensitive records are present


-


Treatment notes do not reference specialists whose records are missing


Codes Health's Missing Record Review compares delivered materials against the original request and patient history, identifying gaps before the record set is treated as complete.


Speed claims deserve the same scrutiny. Codes Health notes that services promising same-day retrieval typically return only what is immediately available electronically, leaving the firm or client to chase the rest, and it says that added client involvement is a common driver of churn.

## **Legal and Ethical Considerations for Handling Medical Records in Omaha**


### **Nebraska Statutory Framework**


**Nebraska §71-8403** establishes patient access rights. For a written request for copies governed by that section, the provider must furnish the copies no later than 30 days after receiving the request. Requests to examine records follow a different, shorter timeline with limited delay provisions.


**Nebraska §71-8404** generally permits up to a $20 handling fee and $0.50 per page for covered requests, subject to statutory exceptions and reasonable additional costs for records that cannot be routinely photocopied, such as X-rays. Different federal fee limits may apply to requests made under HIPAA's individual right of access.


**Nebraska §48-120(4)** requires medical and hospital information relevant to a work injury to be made available on demand to specified workers' compensation parties, and removes privilege for that relevant information in a workers' compensation claim.


### **HIPAA Provisions Relevant to PI Lawyers**


Under[45 CFR 164.512(l)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-C/part-164/subpart-E/section-164.512) , covered entities may disclose protected health information for workers' compensation purposes to the extent authorized by applicable law. For other personal injury matters, an authorization is generally required unless records come through qualifying judicial process. A subpoena that is not accompanied by a court order must satisfy HIPAA's notice or qualified-protective-order requirements under 45 CFR 164.512(e) before a covered entity may disclose.


### **Protecting Client Confidentiality**


Law firms should protect client medical information with appropriate confidentiality and information-security controls. HIPAA applies directly when an organization qualifies as a covered entity or business associate; attorneys may separately be subject to professional, contractual, court-imposed, and other privacy obligations. ## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **How long does it take to receive medical records in Omaha for a personal injury case?**


It depends on the facility and submission method. For a written request for copies under Nebraska §71-8403, the provider must furnish copies no later than 30 days after receipt. Nebraska Medicine says its authorization process may take up to three business days after receipt, with an additional 7 to 10 days for postal delivery when records are mailed. Methodist advises allowing 30 days. VA requests may take up to 20 business days. Facilities handling high volumes or older paper records can take longer.


### **Can a personal injury lawyer request records without a signed authorization?**


Generally no. Most disclosures to attorneys require a valid authorization. Workers' compensation is treated differently: Nebraska §48-120(4) requires medical and hospital information relevant to the work injury to be made available on demand to specified parties, and HIPAA permits workers' compensation disclosures to the extent authorized by applicable law. Records may also come through qualifying judicial process, though a subpoena without a court order must satisfy HIPAA's notice or qualified-protective-order requirements.


### **What Nebraska regulations affect medical record requests?**


Nebraska §71-8403 sets patient access rights and the 30-day deadline for furnishing copies under a qualifying written request. Nebraska §71-8404 caps covered requests at a $20 handling fee and $0.50 per page, with exceptions and permitted additional costs for records that cannot be routinely photocopied. Nebraska §48-120(4) governs workers' compensation disclosures. These operate alongside federal HIPAA requirements.


### **What if a provider does not respond within the statutory timeframe?**


Document every submission and follow-up attempt. Escalate to the facility's compliance officer or patient advocate, citing the applicable Nebraska provision. If the provider stays unresponsive, a formal demand letter is the next step, and legal remedies may be available depending on the circumstances. Persistent follow-up protocols help prevent requests from going quiet in the first place, which is much of what a retrieval service is for.
